content:
Just for future reference (if anyone asks "is math in Lean fundamentally the same as math in set theory?"), I summarized results about equivalence (of various types) between Lean and set theoretic foundations I know below.

Definitions:

  • a set theoretic statement is a first-order logic sentence in which the only predicates are === and ∈\in∈.
  • To say a set theoretic statement ϕ\phiϕ holds in VκV_{\kappa}Vκ​ in a certain theory LLL is to say the relativization of ϕ\phiϕ to VκV_\kappaVκ​ holds in LLL. We also write L⊢(Vκ⊨ϕ)L \vdash (V_\kappa \vDash \phi)L⊢(Vκ​⊨ϕ).
  • Similarly, to say that a set theoretic statement ϕ\phiϕ holds in ZFSet.{u} in Lean is to say that the relativization of ϕ\phiϕ to ZFSet.{u} holds in Lean, and we also write Lean⊢(ZFSet.{u}⊨ϕ)\mathsf{Lean} \vdash (\mathsf{ZFSet}.\{u\} \vDash \phi)Lean⊢(ZFSet.{u}⊨ϕ).
  • Note that "ϕ\phiϕ holds in ZFSet.{u}" can be a Lean statement, and not just a statement in the megalanguage. Similarly, ϕ\phiϕ holds i.e. Vκ⊨ϕV_\kappa \vDash \phiVκ​⊨ϕ can itself be a set theoretic statement (∀x(x∈Vκ→(⋯ ))\forall x (x \in V_{\kappa} \to (\cdots))∀x(x∈Vκ​→(⋯))), and not a statement in the metalanguage.
  • ZFCω means ZFC + {there exists n inaccessible cardinals | n is a natural number}. The foundation is sometimes also known as "ZFC+countable inaccessible cardinals" but the foundation doesn't give you the ability to collect all these inaccessible cardinals into a single set. And ZFCω is not the same as "ZFC + infinitely many inaccessibles", the latter being strictly stronger in consistency strength.
  • PFIRS means parameter-free inaccessible reflection scheme. That's to say, PFIRS is an axiom schema that says that for every set theoretic statement φ\varphiφ, φ→∃κ(Inacc(κ)∧Vκ⊨φ)\varphi \to \exist \kappa (\mathrm{Inacc}(\kappa) \land V_\kappa \vDash \varphi)φ→∃κ(Inacc(κ)∧Vκ​⊨φ), where Vκ⊨φV_\kappa \vDash \varphiVκ​⊨φ should be understood as the relativization of φ\varphiφ to VκV_\kappaVκ​, as said above. ZFC+PFIRS is a strict superset of ZFCω.
  • A statement in the form of Vκ⊨ϕV_\kappa \vDash \phiVκ​⊨ϕ (as above, this is to be understood as a relativization) is local here. An arbitrary set theoretic statement is global.

Equivalence theorem of local set theoretic statements

Source: here, see the discussion after "let me spell out my understanding ot it". Ultimately from Mario's model of Lean in ZFCω, as said in the stackexchange link.

We have the following metatheorem: suppose ϕ\phiϕ is a set theoretic statement. Then Lean proves that ϕ\phiϕ holds in ZFSet.{n}, if and only if, for some lll, ZFC proves that "if κ\kappaκ is an inaccessible cardinal greater than n−1n-1n−1 other inaccessible cardinals and less than lll other inaccessible cardinals, then ϕ\phiϕ holds in VκV_\kappaVκ​". The same for ZFCω and ZFC+PFIRS.

This metatheorem means that Lean and ZFC (with or without countable inaccessible cardinals or PFIRS) have the same local set theoretic consequences.

I think there should be no difficulty generalizing the first metatheorem to the case of multiple universe levels, something like ∀x:ZFSet.{u},∃y:ZFSet.{v}⋯\forall x : \mathsf{ZFSet}.\{u\}, \exist y : \mathsf{ZFSet} .\{v\} \cdots∀x:ZFSet.{u},∃y:ZFSet.{v}⋯, where the ZFSets in the statement are translated to VκV_{\kappa}Vκ​'s, and the translation is still bidirectional. (Am I right here?)

Equivalence theorem of global set theoretic statements

Source: see here, especially see Elliot's posts.

We have the following metatheorem: suppose ϕ\phiϕ is a set theoretic statement. Then ZFC+PFIRS proves ϕ\phiϕ, if and only if, there exists a natural number n such that Lean proves that "for every universe level uuu, ϕ\phiϕ holds in ZFSet.{u}\mathsf{ZFSet}.\{u\}ZFSet.{u}, or ϕ\phiϕ holds in ZFSet.{u+1}\mathsf{ZFSet}.\{u+1\}ZFSet.{u+1}, or ... or ϕ\phiϕ holds in ZFSet.{u+n−1}\mathsf{ZFSet}.\{u+n-1\}ZFSet.{u+n−1}".

Note: uuu is a universe parameter (in Lean, not a metatheoretic concept). What nnn exactly is depends on the structure of ϕ\phiϕ, but it doesn't need to be greater than 1 + the number of PFIRS invocations in proving ϕ\phiϕ in ZFC+PFIRS. This fact follows from how the metatheorem is proven.

Note that in this metatheorem, the ZFC+PFIRS side is "ZFC+PFIRS proves ϕ\phiϕ" and not "ϕ\phiϕ holds in a certain universe". Thus, this metatheorem is about equivalence of global set theoretic statements, and not local statements.

Now obviously Lean doesn't have global set theoretic statements, so what is proven is a connection between statements about ZFSet in Lean and global set theoretic statements in ZFC+PFIRS. No such direct connection exists between statements about ZFSet in Lean and global set theoretic statements in ZFCω. For a concrete example, which can be proven in ZFSet.{0} but not as a global set theoretic theorem in ZFCω, see Elliot's tweet.

Generic equivalence theorem

Source: well known, see Mario's master thesis, and the famous paper Sets in Types, Types in Sets.

We have the following metatheorem: a Lean statement, which does not need to be a set theoretic statement in a ZFSet, can always be translated to a ZFCω via a largely intuitive set theoretic semantics of type systems, and a ZFCω statement (using a finite number of inaccessibles; this system doesn't given you the ability to deal with countable inaccessibles at the same time because there's no way to collect all of them into a single set) can be translated to Lean by using a sufficiently high ZFSet.

This metatheorem is different from the two equivalence metatheorems above in that this metatheorem does not allow translation round trips, while the two metatheorems above do. If there exists n successive universe levels such that Lean proves that ϕ\phiϕ holds in at least one of ZFSets at these universe levels, then ϕ\phiϕ is provable in ZFC+PFIRS, and if vice versa. And yet if ϕ\phiϕ is not a set theoretic statement but a generic Lean statement, something like "for every n:Natn : \mathsf{Nat}n:Nat, there exists x:Realx : \mathsf{Real}x:Real, ..." then by this most well known equivalence metatheorem, in ϕ\phiϕ's counterpart in ZFCω, Nat and Real are translated to their set theoretic encodings. And thus when ϕ\phiϕ is translated back to Lean, it becomes a set theoretic statement's relativization to ZFSet, something like "for every n:ZFSet.{0}n: \mathsf{ZFSet}.\{0\}n:ZFSet.{0}, if n∈Natn \in \mathsf{Nat}n∈Nat (where Nat:ZFSet.{0}\mathsf{Nat} : \mathsf{ZFSet}.\{0\}Nat:ZFSet.{0}), then there exists y:ZFSet.{0}y : \mathsf{ZFSet}.\{0\}y:ZFSet.{0}, such that y∈Realy \in \mathsf{Real}y∈Real, ... We see a bump of the universe level (in the original ϕ\phiϕ, all types are in Type 0, while in the new ϕ\phiϕ, all types are in Type 1.) Now this statement can be thrown back and forth between Lean and ZFCω with its structure preserved but it has a form rather different from what is considered idiomatic in Lean.

Discussion

From the third metatheorem, it immediately follows that Lean and ZFCω are equiconsistent. It then follows that Lean and ZFC+PFIRS are equiconsistent (see here.

However equiconsistency does not mean the two systems behave similarly, and this is a topic explored by the three metatheorems above. That's to say,

  • There is a structure preserving round-trip translation between set theoretic statements in ZFSet in Lean (that may have more than one universe parameters, if I'm not mistaken above) and local set theoretic statements in ZFC+PFIRS.
  • There is a structure preserving round-trip translation between set theoretic statements in ZFSet in Lean (with only one universe parameter, obviously) and global set theoretic statements in ZFC+PFIRS. (Note that in the existing metatheorm, the Lean version of the set theoretic statement ϕ\phiϕ is the disjunction of multiple relativizations of ϕ\phiϕ to ZFSets, but the number of ZFSets can be determined by counting how many times PFIRS is used in the proof of ϕ\phiϕ in ZFC+PFIRS).
  • All Lean statements, not just the ZFSet-centric ones, can be translated to ZFC+PFIRS (or ZFCω). They do not preserve their original forms when translated back, but after a round trip (using metatheorem 3), the resulting set theoretic statements in ZFSet in Lean can then undergo structure-preserving round trips (using metatheorem 1, i.e. translation of local set theoretic statements).

I think intuitively, the third result guarantees that all Lean statements can be mentally conceived as roughly set theoretic, and we should not worry that two formalizations of the same thing using the same rough idea in idiomatic Lean and in ZFCω (or ZFSet-centric Lean) somehow have fundamentally different consequences. This should partially answer the question I raised at the start of this post. (Of course, the ZFCω formalization corresponding to the Lean formalization isn't necessarily the conventional set theoretic formalization, but it's a problem that already exists even without Lean.)

The remaining question is, there is a route from an idiomatic Lean statement to a ZFSet-centric Lean statement, but there is no way back. This is a question that has been explored here. Arithmetic statements can indeed be brought back from a set theoretic foundation to Lean, but that's not the case for everything else.

Elliot's example given in his tweet shows that we can't strike out "ZFC+PFIRS" and insert "ZFCω" in the global equivalence metatheorem, because in Lean, "if there is a proper class of inaccessibles, then Con(TG)" holds in ZFSet.{0}, but this statement can't hold in ZFCω: TG contains the whole ZFCω, and if this statement is provable in ZFCω, it's also provable in TG, which allows TG to prove its own consistency and this is absurd.

Perhaps a more indirect connection between global statements in ZFCω and statements in Lean exists, but currently no one has proven it.

content:
François G. Dorais said:

I think I skipped some beats... What is ZFCω again?

The notation is from here. It means "ZFC + {there are n inaccessible cardinals | n < ω }. This is also the notation used in Mario's master thesis (see Sec. 1.2).

I would have guessed "ZFC + infinitely many inaccessibles".

There's a serious gotcha there. It's tempting to identify universe levels with Nat. But, ZFCω plus this identification implies "ZFC + infinitely many inaccessibles", which is strictly stronger in consistency strength. (Standard disclaimer: in most probable precise interpretations of these words.)

The idea here is the same as the fact that ZFCω has no well-founded model where "there are infinitely many inaccessibles" is false.

François G. Dorais said:

"ZFC + infinitely many inaccessibles", which is strictly stronger in consistency strength

I've just added the caveat to my post above. Thank you for pointing it out!

It's a bit more subtle. You can always collect all inaccessibles up to some bound $\kappa$ into a set. That's just the comprehension axiom working. What happens in models of ZFCω where there is no infinite set of inaccessibles is that the internal ω is nonstandard and there is a nonstandard $n$ for which "there are $n$ inacessibles" is true in the model. From the outside perspective, where we realize that $n$ is nonstandard, we see that ZFCω is true in this model, but the model still believes that "there are finitely many inaccessibles".

Subtleties like that are the reason why we shouldn't expect a level-by-level comparison between type-based theories and set-based theories. What is a natural theory for one probably doesn't translate exactly into a natural theory for the other.

Just to double check, does that mean anything I wrote above is problematic?

Not really, I suppose. The only "problem" is the implicit (but not deliberate) suggestion that ZFCω is a "set theory that set theorists should care about". Because it's "unnatural" from a set theoretic perspective, it's unlikely that set theorists will ever care much about ZFCω.

Do you consider ZFC+PFIRS more "natural"? This question is important especially considering that it appears to capture Lean's set theoretic behaviors better (as in Elliot's global metatheorem discussed above).

The PF part is unusual from a set theoretic perspective, but it is not unprecedented. It's the kind of theory that proof theorists who study set theories would care about. So the intersection of set theorists and proof theorists is the very rare but not empty class of mathematicians who would "naturally" care about ZFC+PFIRS.

I've been arguing for a while that type theories like MLTT, CIC, and Lean's TT should evolve beyond an ω-like universe hierarchy and embrace broader possibilities approaching the point where universe levels are more and more "indiscernable" (in the model-theoretic sense) and therefore progressively irrelevant. This is, in part, what has guided the very fruitful area of large cardinal hypotheses in set theory.
